signals.headline: BC Hydro’s Data Centre Power Picks Are Still Pending, and the Okanagan Is Shut Out
signals.theFact: BC Hydro has still not announced which of the nearly 800 MW of data centre applications will share its 400 MW allocation, after results expected in September were postponed by the provincial election. iNFOnews reports the call excludes FortisBC service areas, which cover much of the Okanagan and are already nearing power capacity, and that the province has restricted BC Hydro from supplying extra power to wholesalers like FortisBC for new data centres.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls targets sub-10 MW brownfield sites that sit outside the ≥10 MW competitive call, so projects can move through BC Hydro’s standard interconnection process instead of waiting on a rationed, delayed allocation.

signals.headline: Memphis Splits 6–6 on a Data Centre Moratorium, Then Bans Evaporative Cooling
signals.theFact: Memphis City Council denied a 12-month moratorium on new data centres on a 6–6 vote, at a meeting that drew more residents than the 407 allowed inside the chambers. The council instead passed an ordinance for large-scale data centres that prohibits routine evaporative and once-through cooling, requires closed-loop water circulation, and bars major withdrawals of local water for cooling.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls places closed-loop or air-cooled sub-10 MW MicroClusters on already-zoned brownfield industrial land, the small, low-water footprint that rules like these are pushing the industry toward.

signals.headline: Ottawa’s $890M Sovereign AI Supercomputer Is Still Unawarded as Budget 2026 Nears
signals.theFact: Five months after applications closed on June 1, the federal program funding Canada’s $890 million public AI supercomputer still hasn’t announced an award, and Signal49 Research notes that seven of the eight cloud vendors approved for federal use are American. The AI Compute Access Fund currently covers 67 cents on the dollar for Canadian compute versus 50 cents for foreign compute, with Budget 2026 due November 5.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Canadian organizations that need sovereign inference now don’t have to wait on a national megaproject: Ocean Falls’ MicroNode puts Canadian-controlled AI compute directly behind their own firewall in British Columbia.

signals.headline: Aon Sees $100B+ in New Data Centre Premiums, but Risk Accumulation Is the Real Struggle
signals.theFact: Aon’s global head of property, Ryan Barber, said data centres could generate more than $100 billion in new insurance premiums over the next five to 10 years, and that placements above $10 billion are now likely possible after an $8.5 billion placement over a year ago. He said the biggest struggle for insurers and reinsurers is tracking the accumulation of builders risk, operational property, equipment and power exposures at the same phased campuses.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls’ distributed sub-10 MW sites avoid single-campus accumulation, and its AI Infrastructure Captive Program covers the AI infrastructure risks traditional insurers won’t take.

signals.headline: BC Hydro’s 2026 AI Power Intake Closes Nearly 2x Oversubscribed as ≥10 MW Projects Hit Election Delay
signals.theFact: Under British Columbia’s Industrial Electricity Allocation Framework, all AI and data centre projects requesting 10 MW or more were forced into BC Hydro’s competitive 2026 Call for Demand, which attracted 15 applications requesting nearly 800 MW against a two-year cap of just 400 MW (300 MW for AI and 100 MW for conventional data centres). While projects under 10 MW remain eligible for BC Hydro’s standard interconnection process, large-load applicants now face rationed grid capacity and an extended decision timeline pushed past the provincial transition.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: By targeting sub-10 MW brownfield industrial sites and behind-the-meter enterprise MicroNodes, Ocean Falls bypasses BC Hydro’s oversubscribed ≥10 MW competitive auction entirely and connects through the standard utility pathway.

signals.headline: Quinte West Rejects Data Centre Pause After Packed Council Meeting
signals.theFact: Quinte West Council defeated, on an 8–5 recorded vote, an Interim Control By-Law that would have paused new data centres for up to one year, after one of the most-attended meetings in municipal history. First Block pledged no city water for cooling and Ontario noise limits at the former Sonoco paper mill, while True North Sustainable Infrastructure said Canadian designs use closed-loop cooling and that the former Saputo site would meet strict noise limits.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls uses sub-10 MW brownfield siting, placing closed-loop or air-cooled MicroClusters on already-zoned industrial land without drawing municipal water for cooling.
